title: There Is a Balm in Gilead
description: The spiritual as R. Nathaniel Dett wrote it down from the singing of Hampton Institute students and printed it in 1927, for 2 to 4 singers. Everyone sings the refrain, twice through, in Dett's own four parts, and between refrains the soprano sings a verse alone: "Sometimes I feel discouraged", then "If you cannot preach like Peter". Slow and very expressive.

licence.arrangement: R. Nathaniel Dett's own four-part refrain as the Hampton Institute Press published it in 1927 (public domain: published 1927; Dett died 1943), a whole tone lower. Every pitch as printed (named here in his B major) but these: the alto sings one note a syllable where it moves with the tune's slurs (F#4 for his F#4 to E4 on "There"); the bass's low F#2 on "sick", under the bass range a tone lower, is sung an octave up, so the bass holds F#3 into "soul.". The fermatas on "whole,", the first "soul." and the verse's "gain." are written out as a held note and an added bar; breaths are written in for beginners ("ad," and the verse's "aged,", "vain," and "it" each give up half a beat); the grace note before the verse's "vain," is left out; the soloist sings the verses alone, as printed, with verse 3's extra syllables ("If you", "You can") on the two halves of the note, as Dett's tied sixteenths show, and "You can say" the same way on "Re-"; the second-ending "soul." before a verse is one beat, and the last one is held three beats. Accepted exceptions (singable.py): R. Nathaniel Dett's own refrain as printed in 1927, as the licence states: the alto's slur up with the tune in the written-out fermata bars, D to F sharp on "whole," and C sharp to F sharp on "soul.", where the tune rises B to D and A to D; and the bass's two fifths in "To heal the sin sick soul.", A up to E on "sin" and back down to A on "soul.", his dominant and tonic, with his low F sharp (here E) on "sick" sung an octave up as the licence notes.
licence.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (Hampton Institute Press, Hampton, Va., 1927), p. 88, "There Is a Balm in Gilead" (Hymns of Consolation), headed "Transcribed from the singing of the Hampton Institute students by R. Nathaniel Dett": a four-part refrain with its repeat, then a solo verse and D.C., with verses 2 and 3 printed below; in B major, 2/4, Andante molto espress, quarter note = 60, written here a whole tone lower in A; sung as the refrain, verse 1, the refrain, verse 3 and the refrain (verse 2 left out for length); the last "He died for all." is printed with an opening quotation mark only, closed here; read from the scan at archive.org/details/religiousfolkson00dett (leaf n119)
